title: Federal and NSW governments to split $2.5 billion Tomago Aluminium bailout

By Ben Clifford

Topic:Mining and Metals Industry

Chris Minns (left) and Anthony Albanese visit the Hunter region to announce a $2.5 billion rescue package for Tomago Aluminium. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

The New South Wales and federal governments have agreed to spend $2.5 billion over 10 years to secure the future of Australia's largest aluminium smelter, Tomago Aluminium.

The smelter's owner, Rio Tinto, threatened closure from 2029 amid the rising cost of renewable and coal-fired power.

Union officials say the deal is a lifeline for Australian manufacturing.

A bailout of the country's largest aluminium smelter will cost taxpayers $2.5 billion, with the New South Wales and federal governments to split the bill down the middle.

Late last year mining giant Rio Tinto warned rising power prices could force the Tomago Aluminium plant to close when its energy supply contract ran out in 2028.

Tomago is currently Australia's largest electricity user, drawing about 10 per cent of the state's total electricity supply annually.

On a visit to the smelter today, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said the long-term renewable energy solution, and its associated price tag, was in the country's "national interest."

Anthony Albanese says the deal will support operations at the site beyond 2028. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

"This is an arrangement that will deliver additional clean energy for New South Wales and for Australia," he said.

"We cannot afford to be at the end of supply chains. We need to be a country that makes things and that is why this [deal] is so important."

The contribution from the NSW government is capped at $1.225 billion over 10 years from 2029.

The smelter's owner, Rio Tinto, will invest a minimum of $1.1 billion on top of the taxpayer funding to reduce its energy usage and gear it toward renewables.

"Would Australia be better off or worse off if these jobs went to Korea, China or India?

"The answer is we would be worse off."

The deal is expected to accelerate the decarbonisation of more than 10 per cent of NSW's electricity grid and underpin nearly 3 gigawatts of new renewable generation.

"This agreement gives Tomago an internationally competitive electricity price, it underpins new renewable energy and, most importantly, it gives Tomago a future," Tomago CEO Jérôme Dozol said.

Tim Ayres says the deal will shore up the long-term future of Australia's aluminium industry. (ABC Newcastle: Bridget Murphy)

Tomago Aluminium produces up to 590,000 tonnes of the metal each year, more than 30 per cent of Australia's total production.

The vast majority of aluminium is shipped across the Asia-Pacific region.

Industry Minister Tim Ayres said today's bailout, which is one of the Albanese government's largest to date, was essential to secure the industry's long-term future.

"Aluminium is a crucial national asset for Australia," he said.

"We're one of the only economies in the world that has an end-to-end aluminium capability.

The rescue package follows a string of similar bailouts the Albanese government has offered to struggling heavy industries, including Glencore's Mount Isa Copper smelter and the Nyrstar smelters in Tasmania and South Australia.

The smelter employs about 1,000 workers and has been operational 24 hours a day since 1983.

Mr Albanese last visited the Hunter site in December 2025, when he told workers he suspected a deal would be reached soon.

However, plans quickly stalled when a clear-cut funding agreement could not be reached with NSW.

The Electrical Trades Union says the deal is a win for Hunter workers and industries. (ABC Newcastle: Nakita Jager)

The Electrical Trades Union (ETU) said today's deal ended months of uncertainty.

"It's been a long time coming," ETU organiser Brad McDougall said.

"New apprentices were left wondering whether they'd get to finish their apprenticeship here.

"This announcement is massive and secures their employment well into the future."

Rio Tinto's latest annual report showed it had recorded a $10 billion profit after tax across 2025, attributable to its owners.

Its total aluminium and lithium projects were valued at $4.6 billion, up from $3.6 billion in 2024.
